Introduction of contaminants into the natural environment that cause harm. Pollution can take the form of any substance (solid, liquid, or gas) or energy such as radioactivity, heat, sound, or light. Although it can be caused by natural events, the word generally implies a human source, such as manufacturing, extractive industries, poor [[Waste management|waste management]], transportation, or agriculture. It is often classed as point source, coming from a concentrated site such as a [[Factory|factory]], mine, or construction site, or nonpoint source, coming from widespread sources such as microplastics or agricultural runoff.

Major forms include [[Air pollution|air pollution]], [[Water pollution|water pollution]], litter, noise pollution, plastic pollution, soil contamination, radioactive contamination, thermal pollution, light pollution, and visual pollution. Common gaseous air pollutants include [[Carbon monoxide|carbon monoxide]], [[Sulfur dioxide|sulfur dioxide]], chlorofluorocarbons, and nitrogen oxides produced by industry and motor vehicles. Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances ([[PFAS]]), informally called "forever chemicals," are a major chemical pollutant.

In 2019, pollution killed approximately nine million people worldwide (about one in six deaths that year); about three-quarters of these deaths were caused by air pollution. Children, the elderly, and marginalized communities bear outsized impacts, a core reason for the environmental justice movement. Many sources went unregulated during 19th- and 20th-century industrialization until environmental regulation emerged in the later half of the 20th century. International efforts are now coordinated by the [[United Nations|UN]] Environmental Program and other treaty bodies.

Plane figure made up of line segments connected to form a closed chain. The segments are its edges or sides, and the points where two edges meet are its vertices or corners. An n-gon has n sides; a [[Triangle|triangle]] is a 3-gon, and a [[Quadrilateral|quadrilateral]] a 4-gon.

A simple polygon does not intersect itself and forms the boundary of a region of the plane called a solid polygon. A chain that crosses itself produces star polygons and other self-intersecting polygons. Some sources also count closed chains in [[Euclidean space]] that do not lie in a single plane (skew polygons). A polygon is the 2-dimensional example of the more general polytope.

Polygons are classified by number of sides, convexity, and symmetry. In a convex polygon, any line through it that is not tangent to an edge or corner meets the boundary exactly twice, and all interior angles are less than 180°. A concave polygon is simple but has at least one interior angle greater than 180°. A regular polygon has equal angles and equal edges. A cyclic polygon has all corners on a single [[Circle|circle]], the circumcircle.

The interior angles of a simple n-gon sum to (n − 2) × 180°, because it can be divided into (n − 2) triangles. The exterior angles of a convex polygon sum to 360°; in general the sum can be any integer multiple of 360°, such as 720° for a [[Pentagram|pentagram]]. Polygons form the basis of polygonal meshes in [[Computer graphics|computer graphics]], of tiling in architecture, and of boundaries in geographic information systems.

Subregion of [[Oceania]] made up of more than 1,000 islands scattered over the central and southern [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]]. Its indigenous inhabitants, the Polynesians, share linguistic relations, cultural practices, and traditional beliefs. The French writer Charles de Brosses first used the term *Polynésie* in 1756 for all the Pacific islands; in 1831 Jules Dumont d'Urville proposed a narrower definition. The region is generally defined as the islands within the Polynesian Triangle, drawn by connecting Hawaii, [[New Zealand]], and [[Easter Island]]. The [[Hawaiian Islands]] lie at its northern vertex. Other main groups inside it include Samoa, Tonga, the Cook Islands, Tuvalu, and French Polynesia. Outliers lie in [[Melanesia]] and Micronesia.

Polynesia has about 300,000 to 310,000 sq km of land, of which more than 270,000 sq km are in New Zealand; the Hawaiian archipelago makes up about half the remainder. Most islands, including the Hawaiian Islands and Samoa, are volcanic islands built by hotspots. New Zealand, Norfolk Island, and Ouvéa are unsubmerged portions of the largely sunken continent of [[Zealandia]], believed to have mostly sunk below sea level 23 million years ago.

Polynesians trace their ancestry to Austronesian-speaking peoples from Island Southeast Asia who reached the Samoa-Tonga-Fiji area around 3,000 years before present as part of the Lapita cultural complex. Settlement of remote outliers such as Hawaii and Rapa Nui was complete by about 1200 CE. Polynesian societies shared chiefly hierarchies and oral genealogies. Their [[Navigation|wayfinding]] drew on stars, ocean swells, winds, and birds, and double-hulled voyaging canoes sustained long-distance exchange between islands.

Genre of popular music that originated in its modern form during the mid-1950s in the United States and the United Kingdom. During the 1950s and 1960s it encompassed [[Rock and roll|rock and roll]] and the youth-oriented styles it influenced. Rock and pop remained roughly synonymous until the late 1960s; from about 1967 the term was increasingly used in opposition to [[Rock music|rock music]], which aspired to authenticity and an expansion of the possibilities of popular music, while pop became more commercial, ephemeral, and accessible.

According to *The New Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians*, "pop music" originated in Britain in the mid-1950s as a description for rock and roll and the new youth styles it influenced; in the early 1960s it competed with beat music in England. The *Oxford Dictionary of Music* says that since the late 1950s pop has meant non-classical music, usually songs, by artists such as [[The Beatles]], [[The Rolling Stones]], and [[ABBA]].

Typical features are repeated choruses and hooks, short to medium-length songs in a basic format (often verse–chorus), and rhythms that can easily be danced to. Songs are often two and a half to three and a half minutes long. Pop borrows from rock, [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]], dance, Latin, and country, and its roots include Tin Pan Alley songwriting, [[Blues|blues]], and gospel. Scholar Timothy Warner describes an emphasis on recording, production, and technology over live performance. Musicologist Simon Frith calls pop music produced "as a matter of enterprise not art," by the [[Music industry|music industry]]. Analyses of the Billboard Hot 100 charts from 1960 to 2010 identify stylistic revolutions around 1964, 1983, and 1991.

Set of practices, beliefs, artistic output, and objects that are dominant or prevalent in a society at a given time; also called pop culture or mass culture. [[Mass media]], marketing, and the imperatives of mass appeal within capitalism are the primary engines of Western popular culture, a system the philosopher Theodor Adorno critically termed the "culture industry." It is generally contrasted with folk culture, working-class culture, or high culture, and is defined in conflicting ways, including from [[Postmodernism|postmodernist]] perspectives.

The phrase was coined in the 19th century or earlier and was traditionally associated with poor education and the lower classes, as opposed to the "official culture" of the upper classes. During the [[Industrial Revolution]], Britain experienced rising literacy and growing spending on entertainment such as public houses and sports. The first penny serials were published in the 1830s. After World War II, mass media innovations made the term overlap with mass culture, media culture, and consumer culture. The abbreviated form pop, as in [[Pop music|pop music]], dates from the late 1950s and is narrower, referring to mass appeal rather than mere popularity.

From the 1970s, Japan became a global source of popular culture through [[Sony]] and Matsushita (now Panasonic), the Walkman, and kawaii culture, the "cult of cute," fronted by companies such as Sanrio and [[Nintendo]]. Characters such as [[Hello Kitty]] spread to East Asia and the West.

According to the author John Storey, definitions vary: culture that is widely liked, culture left over once high culture is decided, mass-produced commercial culture, or an "authentic" culture of the people. Neo-Gramscian theory sees it as a site of struggle between subordinate and dominant groups.

Western Romance language of the Indo-European language family. With approximately 267 million native speakers, it is the fifth-most spoken native language in the world and the most widely spoken in the Southern Hemisphere. It is the official language of eight countries: [[Portugal]], [[Brazil]], [[Angola]], [[Mozambique]], Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Príncipe, and Timor-Leste. It is co-official with other languages in [[Macau]] and [[Equatorial Guinea]].

Portuguese belongs to the Ibero-Romance group, which evolved from dialects of Vulgar [[Latin]] in the medieval Kingdom of Galicia and the County of Portugal, and it retains some Celtic phonology. The Roman presence in the Iberian Peninsula began in 218 BC. In Gallaecia, the northwest, Vulgar Latin lost intervocalic *l* and *n* (*luna* to *lua*) and simplified double consonants (*annu* to *ano*). Between the 9th and 12th centuries the language emerged as Galician-Portuguese; the earliest known Portuguese document, the *Notícia de Fiadores*, dates to 1175. King Denis (1279–1325) promoted its use in literature and administration. Maritime expansion in the 15th and 16th centuries carried it to Africa, Asia, and the Americas.

Its [[Phonology|phonology]] has a rich system of nasal vowels and varied guttural *r* sounds. Spelling uses the Latin alphabet and is largely phonemic. Grammar retains many Latin verb forms and has unusual features such as the future subjunctive and the personal infinitive. Vocabulary is largely Latin, with loanwords from Celtic, Germanic, Arabic, African, Amerindian, and Asian languages.

The two main standardized varieties are European Portuguese and Brazilian Portuguese, each with regional accents. African and Asian varieties generally follow the European written standard. The varieties are broadly mutually intelligible, and a 1990 orthographic agreement sought a unified spelling.

Period of world history from about 500 to about 1450 or 1500, roughly corresponding to the European [[Middle Ages]] after the decline of the Western Roman Empire. It is also called the medieval era, post-antiquity era, post-ancient era, or pre-modern era. The post-classical period is marked by the geographic expansion of certain civilizations, ongoing wars over land, resources, and religion, and the development of trade networks between distant civilizations.

The term is a periodization used by world historians, a school developed in the late 20th and early 21st centuries, and is one of five or six major periods: early civilization, classical societies, post-classical, early modern, the long nineteenth century, and the contemporary era. Its start varies by region, following the end of Han China (220), the Western Roman Empire (476), the Gupta Empire (543), and the Sasanian Empire (651). Some historians use it to avoid preconceptions attached to the terms Middle Ages and Dark Ages, though applying it globally is problematic and may be Eurocentric.

In Asia and the Middle East, the spread of Islam produced a series of caliphates that fostered the [[Islamic Golden Age]], with advances in science and greater trade among Asia, Africa, and Europe. East Asia saw the entrenchment of a unitary imperial China, whose dynastic governance and culture influenced Japan, Korea, and Vietnam. Buddhism and neo-Confucianism spread there, while Christianity became entrenched in Europe. [[Gunpowder]] was developed in China. The [[Mongol Empire]], which one account dates 1206–1368, conquered much of Europe and Asia and permitted more trade and cultural exchange along the [[Silk Road]]. In West Africa the Mali and Songhai Empires formed, and in the Americas Mesoamerican and Andean civilizations developed complex urban centers. In Western Europe, the fall of Rome gave way to [[Feudalism|feudalism]] and manorialism, while the Eastern Roman Empire (Byzantium) retained many features of old Rome.

World population broadly doubled, from approximately 210 million in 500 to some 461 million in 1500. Growth was slow, with high mortality and rapid declines caused by events including the Plague of Justinian, the Mongol invasions, and the [[Black Death]] (1347–1351). Some commentators view the history of the Earth's climate as a useful approach, noting that certain climate events affected all human populations.

Starchy tuberous vegetable native to the Americas, eaten as a staple food in many parts of the world. Potatoes are underground stem tubers of *Solanum tuberosum*, a perennial in the nightshade family [[Solanaceae]]. Wild species occur from the southern United States to southern Chile. The cultivated potato has a single origin in present-day southern Peru and extreme northwestern Bolivia, around [[Lake Titicaca]], where it was domesticated about 7,000–10,000 years ago from a species in the *S. brevicaule* complex.

The plant is a herbaceous perennial growing up to one metre high. Its tubers are stems, not roots, and form in response to decreasing day length. Like the [[Tomato|tomato]], it belongs to the genus *Solanum*. The major cultivated species, *S. tuberosum*, is a tetraploid with 48 [[Chromosome|chromosomes]].

The Spanish introduced the potato to Europe in the second half of the 16th century, following the [[Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire]], as part of the [[Columbian exchange]]. European and colonial farmers were slow to adopt it, but after 1750 it became an important food staple and field crop and played a major role in the 19th-century European population boom. After centuries of [[Selective breeding|selective breeding]] there are over 5,000 varieties. Per capita production is highest in Northern and Eastern Europe, while the most rapid 21st-century expansion has been in southern and eastern Asia, with China and India leading world production as of 2023.

The aerial parts contain the toxin solanine, and tubers exposed to light, especially sprouts and skins, can become toxic. The English word comes from Spanish *patata*, from Taíno *batata*, which meant [[Sweet potato|sweet potato]].

Craft and products of forming vessels and other objects from [[Clay|clay]] and other raw materials, fired at high temperatures to give them a hard and durable form. Firing, at 600–1,400 °C in a bonfire, pit, or kiln, causes permanent changes that increase strength and rigidity. End uses include tableware, decorative ware, sanitary ware, and electrical insulators. Some pottery is regarded as [[Ceramic art|ceramic art]]. In art history and archaeology, pottery often means only vessels, and sculpted figurines of the same material are called terracottas.

It is one of the oldest human inventions, originating before the [[Neolithic]] period. The earliest known vessels, from Jiangxi, [[China]], date to 18,000 BC. Other early finds come from the Russian Far East (14,000 BC), Jōmon Japan (10,500 BC), and Sub-Saharan Africa (9,400 BC). Early methods were hand-building, by pinching or coiling clay; the [[Potter's wheel|potter's wheel]] was invented in [[Mesopotamia]] around 3500 BC.

Pottery is traditionally divided into earthenware, stoneware, and porcelain, each of which may be glazed or unglazed. Earthenware, the earliest form, can be fired as low as 600 °C and is normally fired below 1,200 °C; unglazed, it is porous, and reddish varieties are called terracotta. Stoneware, fired at about 1,100–1,200 °C, is non-porous and strong. The Chinese developed it very early, whereas in Europe it could be produced only from the late Middle Ages and remained a speciality of Germany until the Renaissance. [[Porcelain]], made from materials generally including kaolin and fired at 1,200–1,400 °C is tougher, stronger, and translucent. First made in China, it reached considerable whiteness and translucency by the [[Tang dynasty]] (AD 618–906), and the modern level of whiteness came only in the 14th century. Korea and Japan made it from the end of the 16th century.

State in which an individual or community lacks the financial resources and essentials for a basic standard of living. Statisticians and economists use two main measures. Absolute poverty compares income against the amount needed to meet basic needs such as food, clothing, and shelter; relative poverty applies when a person cannot meet a minimum level of living standards compared with others in the same time and place, and its definition varies between societies. The "dollar a day" line, introduced in 1990, is set by [[Purchasing power parity]] rather than market exchange rates.

Definitions differ by institution. The [[United Nations|UN]] describes poverty as "a denial of choices and opportunities, a violation of human dignity." The [[European Union]] measures it relative to each member country's income distribution. As of 2019, 85% of people lived on less than $30 per day in purchasing power parity dollars, two-thirds on less than $10, and 10% on less than $1.90.

Gender, disability, race, and ethnicity can exacerbate poverty, with women, children, and minorities frequently bearing unequal burdens. Poor people are more vulnerable to climate change and natural disasters, and economic pressure on poor communities frequently contributes to [[Deforestation|deforestation]], biodiversity loss, and [[Ethnic conflict|ethnic conflict]]. Governments and [[Non-governmental organization|non-governmental organizations]] have tried policies such as rural electrification. The UN's 2015 framework for poverty alleviation is Sustainable Development Goal 1, "No Poverty."

Extreme poverty is estimated to have afflicted over 90% of humanity in 1820 and under 10% today, a decline some analysts credit to economic growth in regions such as East Asia. Analysts disagree on causes, and some argue that relative definitions tied to national medians conflate inequality with destitution.
